Party Acquaintances

Graph TheoryLogicCounting
Game: Six people at a party: join each pair with a red line if they know each other and a blue line if they don't. Can you avoid three who all know each other and three who are all strangers?
How to play: Click one person, then another, to draw a line. The colours take turns, or pick them yourself.
Look for the math

At any party of six, either three people all know each other or three are all strangers. Colour each of the 15 lines of the complete graph K6 red or blue: a one-colour triangle always appears. This is the smallest case of Ramsey's theorem.

Why six is enough

Take one person. Of the other five, at least three are joined to them in the same colour, say red. If any two of those three are joined in red, that makes a red triangle with the first person. If not, the three are joined to each other all in blue: a blue triangle. The logic test checked all 32,768 colourings of K6. Every one has a one-colour triangle, and in fact at least two (A. W. Goodman).

Why five is not

Seat five people at a round table and let each know only the two neighbours: red is the pentagon, blue the five-pointed star, and neither has a triangle. (Only 12 of the 1,024 colourings of K5 manage this.) So the Ramsey number is R(3, 3) = 6. Use #Red and #Blue to look for larger groups: R(4, 3) = 9, R(5, 3) = 14, R(4, 4) = 18.

Bounds, and a slip on the original page

Splitting everyone else by their colour to one person shows R(m, n) ≤ R(m−1, n) + R(m, n−1), and hence R(m, n) ≤ C(m+n−2, m−1). Lower bounds need clever colourings. For R(5, 3) > 13 the original page seats 13 people who each know only the fifth person on either side. That does avoid three acquaintances, but people 1 to 5 sitting together are then five mutual strangers. If each person also knows both neighbours, both conditions hold. The test checked this, and also the colourings showing R(4, 3) > 8 and R(4, 4) > 17.

Set N to 5 and draw the round table: pentagon red, star blue. Then set N to 6 and try to escape.
